input: This passage reports the performance of a shell-and-tube heat exchanger that is used to heat crude oil as part of a refinery preheat train, an application in which reliable heat recovery plays an important role in overall energy efficiency. The duty handled by the exchanger is 1062 kW, which is a substantial rate of heat transfer. On the hot side of the unit, the stream enters at a temperature of 150 °C and leaves at 110 °C, while on the cold side the crude stream enters at 25 °C and is heated to an outlet temperature of 40 °C. Based on these terminal temperatures, the log-mean temperature difference for the exchanger works out at 97 K, and this value, taken together with the installed heat-transfer area of 43.1 m2, leads to an overall heat-transfer coefficient of 254 W m-2 K-1. It is worth noting, however, that the assessment of fouling in the unit was based on a single 90-day run, which is a relatively limited body of evidence, and no cleaning cycle has been completed as yet, so the longer-term fouling behaviour of the exchanger under service conditions remains to be established in a fuller manner. The reported coefficient should accordingly be treated as a description of the exchanger as it was found during that particular run, rather than as a guaranteed figure for the unit in a cleaned condition or for its behaviour over a much longer period of operation in the preheat train.
target: A shell-and-tube exchanger in a refinery preheat train heats crude oil at a duty of 1062 kW. The hot stream enters at 150 °C and leaves at 110 °C; the crude enters at 25 °C and leaves at 40 °C. Terminal temperatures give a log-mean temperature difference of 97 K. With the installed area of 43.1 m2, the duty corresponds to an overall coefficient of 254 W m-2 K-1. The coefficient is a clean-condition figure in one respect and a service figure in another. It is computed from measured temperatures and the installed area, so it describes the exchanger as run; it is not corrected for the fouling layer that the run itself deposited. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run. No cleaning cycle has been completed, so the run gives one fouling state, at one crude throughput history, with no cleaned baseline measured in the same campaign. The value therefore characterises the exchanger over that run only. A coefficient intended for design margin, or for predicting performance after cleaning, needs the cleaned condition and a second fouling interval, neither of which the present evidence supplies. Terminal temperatures alone cannot separate the two resistances that the single coefficient combines, the film resistance on each side and the fouling resistance between them. Any cleaning decision taken from the present figure would be taken blind: the figure says how far performance sits from the temperature driving force, and it does not say how much of that distance a cleaning cycle would recover. A repeat run after cleaning, at matched throughput, is the measurement that would divide the coefficient into its parts.
